To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the visible optical depth change due to ship tracks in low-level clouds is about half the value expected given changes in droplet radii, (2) the shortfall in the visible optical depth is unlikely to be caused by the absorbing nature of the polluting particles, and (3) the shortfall in visible optical depth is likely caused by the loss of liquid water from the clouds.

the observed changes in visible optical depth are approximately half of the values expected from changes in droplet radii, and that the remaining shortfall in the optical depths is likely to be due to a loss of cloud liquid water.

ship tracks in the marine boundary layer are associated with an increase in cloud droplet number concentration and a decrease in droplets sizes, that the increase in the droplet number concentration is about half of what is expected given the change in droplet sizes and assuming cloud liquid amount remains constant, and that this shortfall is likely due to a loss of cloud liquid water.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the indirect effects of aerosols on clouds.
the indirect effect of aerosols on the radiative properties of clouds, and we find that the indirect effect is limited by a loss of cloud liquid water.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

ship tracks provide evidence that the indirect radiative effect of aerosols on clouds could not be greater than about 50% of the value estimated from theoretical calculations, but that it could be as small as 0‐25% of that value.
the aerosol‐induced change in cloud liquid water is not greater than about 15%‐25% of the initial amount.
the indirect aerosol effects on clouds are less than the maximum value estimated from the ship tracks, which is 0.6 W m ^{−2} for the global annual mean.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the observed changes in cloud droplet sizes are not sufficient to account for the observed changes in visible optical depth.
the maximum change in cloud optical depth due to ship tracks is about 0.1, and this change is accompanied by a 10%‐20% decrease in the liquid water amount.
the maximum possible change in the visible optical depth of low-level clouds due to anthropogenic aerosol increases is 0.1‐0.2, which is about half the change predicted in some models.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the indirect effect of aerosol on clouds may be smaller than previously thought.
the indirect radiative effect of aerosols is likely to be less than that predicted from the assumption of constant liquid water amount.
the aerosol indirect radiative effect, as measured by the change in the cloud albedo, cannot exceed 50%.
